Moment estimation and its limits

A finite sample produces a finite empirical moment in exact arithmetic. It does not establish that the corresponding population moment exists. Even when that moment exists, the estimator can have infinite variance or be dominated by events that most samples miss. We separate these questions using an exact Pareto model and a finite Gaussian mixture.

The sample notation follows the shared canon. For iid Xi≥0X_i\ge0Xi​≥0 and order q>0q>0q>0, write

mq=EXq,m^q,n=1n∑i=1nXiq.\begin{aligned} m_q&=\mathbb E X^q,\\ \widehat m_{q,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^q. \end{aligned}mq​mq,n​​=EXq,=n1​i=1∑n​Xiq​.​
(1)

These are raw moments. For a signed variable, replace XqX^qXq by ∣X∣q|X|^q∣X∣q; a signed odd moment requires separate integrability conditions.

The estimator needs a higher moment¶

For Pareto with α,xm>0\alpha,x_m>0α,xm​>0,

mq=αxmqα−q,q<α,mq=∞,q≥α.\begin{aligned} m_q&=\frac{\alpha x_m^q}{\alpha-q},\\ &\hspace{2em}q<\alpha,\\ m_q&=\infty,\\ &\hspace{2em}q\ge\alpha. \end{aligned}mq​mq​​=α−qαxmq​​,q<α,=∞,q≥α.​
(2)

We distinguish existence of the target from variance of its estimator.

Proposition 1 (Pareto sample-moment expectation and variance)

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be iid Pareto Type I observations with xm,α>0x_m,\alpha>0xm​,α>0, let 0<q<α0<q<\alpha0<q<α, and let n≥1n\ge1n≥1 be an integer. Then m^q,n=n−1∑i=1nXiq\widehat m_{q,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^qmq,n​=n−1∑i=1n​Xiq​ is unbiased for mq=αxmq/(α−q)m_q=\alpha x_m^q/(\alpha-q)mq​=αxmq​/(α−q). Its variance is finite exactly when 2q<α2q<\alpha2q<α, in which case

nVar⁡(m^q,n)=αxm2qα−2q−(αxmqα−q)2.\begin{aligned} n\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{q,n}) &=\frac{\alpha x_m^{2q}}{\alpha-2q}\\ &\quad-\left(\frac{\alpha x_m^q}{\alpha-q}\right)^2. \end{aligned}nVar(mq,n​)​=α−2qαxm2q​​−(α−qαxmq​​)2.​
(3)

For q<α≤2qq<\alpha\le2qq<α≤2q, its variance is infinite; the equality 2q=α2q=\alpha2q=α is the logarithmically divergent boundary.

Proof 1

Linearity gives the expectation whenever mqm_qmq​ is finite. For 2q<α2q<\alpha2q<α, independence makes the cross-covariances zero. For q<α≤2qq<\alpha\le2qq<α≤2q, nonnegativity gives m^q,n2≥X12q/n2\widehat m_{q,n}^2\ge X_1^{2q}/n^2mq,n2​≥X12q​/n2, whose expectation is infinite. Since the estimator has finite mean, its variance is infinite too. Equality at 2q=α2q=\alpha2q=α is excluded by the logarithmic divergence of the Pareto moment integral.

For example, α=3,xm=1\alpha=3,x_m=1α=3,xm​=1 gives m2=3m_2=3m2​=3, but m^2,n\widehat m_{2,n}m2,n​ has infinite variance at every finite nnn. At α=6\alpha=6α=6, m2=3/2m_2=3/2m2​=3/2, m4=3m_4=3m4​=3, and the estimator variance is 3/(4n)3/(4n)3/(4n). A simulated finite standard error in the first model cannot certify the population variance of the estimator.

Consistency does not require estimator variance¶

The integrable weak law applies to the powered observations. Its clipping argument also gives a direct proof of this consequence.

Corollary 1 (Consistency of an integrable empirical moment)

Let Xi≥0X_i\ge0Xi​≥0 be iid and let q>0q>0q>0 with mq=EX1q<∞m_q=\mathbb EX_1^q<\inftymq​=EX1q​<∞. Then m^q,n=n−1∑i=1nXiq→mq\widehat m_{q,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^q\to m_qmq,n​=n−1∑i=1n​Xiq​→mq​ in probability, even if EX12q=∞\mathbb EX_1^{2q}=\inftyEX12q​=∞. For iid real XiX_iXi​, the same conclusion holds for empirical absolute moments when E∣X1∣q<∞\mathbb E|X_1|^q<\inftyE∣X1​∣q<∞.

Proof 2

The integrable weak law Proposition 2 applies to XiqX_i^qXiq​, or ∣Xi∣q|X_i|^q∣Xi​∣q in the signed case. To spell out its argument here, for a fixed truncation level B>0B>0B>0, Chebyshev’s inequality gives convergence of the average of min⁡(Xiq,B)\min(X_i^q,B)min(Xiq​,B) to its expectation, because these variables are bounded and iid. The omitted nonnegative part has expected average E(X1q−B)+→0\mathbb E(X_1^q-B)_+\to0E(X1q​−B)+​→0 as B→∞B\to\inftyB→∞. Markov’s inequality controls that average uniformly in nnn. For any error tolerance, first choose BBB to make this expectation small, then nnn to control the bounded average. The triangle inequality proves m^q,n→mq\widehat m_{q,n}\to m_qmq,n​→mq​ in probability.

This argument supplies no uniform rate over all integrable laws.

When mq=∞m_q=\inftymq​=∞, the stronger almost-sure divergence follows from the nonnegative infinite-mean theorem, applied to XiqX_i^qXiq​. That linked note proves the result by truncation. Finite observed values and floating-point overflow are separate matters; neither determines which population regime applies.

A square root changes the moment question¶

Proposition 2 (Finite variance after taking a square root)

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be iid real observations, n≥1n\ge1n≥1, with m2=EX12<∞m_2=\mathbb EX_1^2<\inftym2​=EX12​<∞, and put m^2,n=n−1∑Xi2\widehat m_{2,n}=n^{-1}\sum X_i^2m2,n​=n−1∑Xi2​ and Rn=m^2,nR_n=\sqrt{\widehat m_{2,n}}Rn​=m2,n​​. Then

ERn2=m2,ERn≤m2,Var⁡(Rn)<∞.\begin{gathered} \mathbb E R_n^2=m_2,\\ \mathbb E R_n\le\sqrt{m_2},\\ \operatorname{Var}(R_n)<\infty. \end{gathered}ERn2​=m2​,ERn​≤m2​​,Var(Rn​)<∞.​
(4)

Also, for sn=n−1∑(Xi−Xˉn)2s_n=\sqrt{n^{-1}\sum(X_i-\bar X_n)^2}sn​=n−1∑(Xi​−Xˉn​)2​, Esn2≤m2\mathbb Es_n^2\le m_2Esn2​≤m2​ and Var⁡(sn)<∞\operatorname{Var}(s_n)<\inftyVar(sn​)<∞. For n>1n>1n>1, multiplying sn2s_n^2sn2​ by n/(n−1)n/(n-1)n/(n−1) preserves these finiteness conclusions.

Proof 3

Linearity gives ERn2=m2\mathbb ER_n^2=m_2ERn2​=m2​. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ERn≤m2\mathbb ER_n\le\sqrt{m_2}ERn​≤m2​​ and finite variance. The identity sn2=m^2,n−Xˉn2≤m^2,ns_n^2=\widehat m_{2,n}-\bar X_n^2\le\widehat m_{2,n}sn2​=m2,n​−Xˉn2​≤m2,n​ gives the same finite-second-moment conclusion for sns_nsn​. A fixed finite correction factor preserves it.

Thus infinite variance of the empirical second moment does not imply infinite variance of the empirical root mean square.

The square root can introduce downward bias through concavity. The sample raw moment remains unbiased. Bias, estimator variance, and the frequency of an underestimate are different properties.

Finite moments that most samples miss¶

Proposition 4 (A finite second moment missed by many samples)

Let the pairs (Yi,Zi)(Y_i,Z_i)(Yi​,Zi​) be iid, with Zi∼N(0,1)Z_i\sim N(0,1)Zi​∼N(0,1) independent of YiY_iYi​, P(Yi=0.5)=0.99P(Y_i=0.5)=0.99P(Yi​=0.5)=0.99 and P(Yi=50.5)=0.01P(Y_i=50.5)=0.01P(Yi​=50.5)=0.01. Put Xi=YiZiX_i=\sqrt{Y_i}Z_iXi​=Yi​​Zi​. Then EXi2=1\mathbb EX_i^2=1EXi2​=1, EXi4=77.25\mathbb EX_i^4=77.25EXi4​=77.25, and Var⁡(n−1∑Xi2)=76.25/n\operatorname{Var}(n^{-1}\sum X_i^2)=76.25/nVar(n−1∑Xi2​)=76.25/n. The event that no wide component is selected has probability 0.99n0.99^n0.99n; conditional on it, the empirical second moment has expectation 0.5.

Proof 6

The two-state mixture calculation gives EY=1\mathbb EY=1EY=1 and EY2=25.75\mathbb EY^2=25.75EY2=25.75. Conditioning gives EX2=EY=1\mathbb EX^2=\mathbb EY=1EX2=EY=1 and EX4=3EY2=77.25\mathbb EX^4=3\mathbb EY^2=77.25EX4=3EY2=77.25. Independence yields the estimator variance (77.25−1)/n(77.25-1)/n(77.25−1)/n. The event probability is the product 0.99n0.99^n0.99n. Conditional on it, the observations are independent N(0,0.5)N(0,0.5)N(0,0.5), giving conditional second-moment expectation 0.5.

At n=50n=50n=50, this event has probability about 0.605. Rare samples compensate in the unconditional mean; the raw second moment estimator is still unbiased.

Fitting a model introduces another boundary¶

The known-cutoff Pareto plug-in uses ξ^n=n−1∑log⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\xi_n=n^{-1}\sum\log(X_i/x_m)ξ​n​=n−1∑log(Xi​/xm​).

Use pareto_mean_plugin.

from xmath.incerto.estimators import pareto_mean_plugin

for sample in ([1, 1], [1, 2], [4, 4]):
    print(f"{sample} {pareto_mean_plugin(sample, x_m=1):.4g}")

Output

[1, 1] 1
[1, 2] 1.53
[4, 4] inf
Proposition 5 (Infinite moments even conditional on a finite Pareto fit)

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be iid Pareto Type I with known cutoff xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, exponent α>1\alpha>1α>1, and integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1. Put ξ^n=n−1∑i=1nlog⁡(Xi/xm)\widehat\xi_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_i/x_m)ξ​n​=n−1∑i=1n​log(Xi​/xm​). Conditional on ξ^n<1\widehat\xi_n<1ξ​n​<1, the finite mean plug-in xm/(1−ξ^n)x_m/(1-\widehat\xi_n)xm​/(1−ξ​n​) has infinite expectation and infinite second moment.

Proof 7

The plug-in note derives the gamma density of ξ^n\widehat\xi_nξ​n​, which is positive and continuous at 1. Its positive lower bound on a small left neighborhood of 1 bounds the conditional first moment below by a positive multiple of ∫1−δ1(1−t)−1 dt=∞\int_{1-\delta}^1(1-t)^{-1}\,dt=\infty∫1−δ1​(1−t)−1dt=∞. The event being conditioned on has positive probability. Replacing the integrand by (1−t)−2(1-t)^{-2}(1−t)−2 proves divergence of the second moment.

A concentrated central part of a sampling distribution can coexist with divergent moments. Simulations must count non-finite fits; removing them does not remove the singularity of the remaining distribution. No universal ranking of the sample mean and this plug-in follows.

Rising power means and different targets¶

Proposition 6 (Weighted power means increase with their order)

Let x1,…,xn∈Rx_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb Rx1​,…,xn​∈R, n≥1n\ge1n≥1, and let wi>0w_i>0wi​>0 with ∑iwi=1\sum_iw_i=1∑i​wi​=1. Define Ap=(∑iwi∣xi∣p)1/pA_p=(\sum_iw_i|x_i|^p)^{1/p}Ap​=(∑i​wi​∣xi​∣p)1/p for p>0p>0p>0. For 0<p<q0<p<q0<p<q, Ap≤AqA_p\le A_qAp​≤Aq​, with equality exactly when all ∣xi∣|x_i|∣xi​∣ are equal. Also Ap→max⁡i∣xi∣A_p\to\max_i|x_i|Ap​→maxi​∣xi​∣ as p→∞p\to\inftyp→∞.

Proof 8

Apply Jensen to the strictly convex function t↦tq/pt\mapsto t^{q/p}t↦tq/p on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) and take a qqqth root. Positive weights give the stated equality condition. At a maximizing coordinate jjj, wj∣xj∣p≤∑iwi∣xi∣p≤∣xj∣pw_j|x_j|^p\le\sum_iw_i|x_i|^p\le|x_j|^pwj​∣xj​∣p≤∑i​wi​∣xi​∣p≤∣xj​∣p. Taking pppth roots and then letting p→∞p\to\inftyp→∞ proves the limit, including the zero-vector case.

The inequality also holds below 1; those expressions are not norms.

For equal weights and observations (0,0,0,4)(0,0,0,4)(0,0,0,4), A1=1A_1=1A1​=1, A2=2A_2=2A2​=2, A4=22A_4=2\sqrt2A4​=22​, and A∞=4A_\infty=4A∞​=4. The order changes which quantity is summarized; a larger value alone neither proves a power law nor diagnoses estimation failure.

Proposition 7 (Unnormalized power sums decrease with their order)

For x∈Rnx\in\mathbb R^nx∈Rn and p>0p>0p>0, put ∥x∥p=(∑i=1n∣xi∣p)1/p\|x\|_p=(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p)^{1/p}∥x∥p​=(∑i=1n​∣xi​∣p)1/p. For 0<p<q0<p<q0<p<q, ∥x∥q≤∥x∥p\|x\|_q\le\|x\|_p∥x∥q​≤∥x∥p​; consequently {x:∥x∥p≤1}⊆{x:∥x∥q≤1}\{x:\|x\|_p\le1\}\subseteq\{x:\|x\|_q\le1\}{x:∥x∥p​≤1}⊆{x:∥x∥q​≤1}. The notation denotes a norm only when p≥1p\ge1p≥1.

Proof 9

The case x=0x=0x=0 is immediate. For x≠0x\ne0x=0, without loss of generality, assume ∥x∥p=1\|x\|_p=1∥x∥p​=1: both expressions scale by the same positive factor when xxx is divided by ∥x∥p\|x\|_p∥x∥p​. Within this argument, xxx now denotes that normalized vector. Its coordinate magnitudes are at most 1, so their qqqth powers sum to at most their pppth powers, namely 1. The ppp-unit balls therefore expand.

In two dimensions, p=1,2,∞p=1,2,\inftyp=1,2,∞ give a diamond, circle, and square, with areas 2, π\piπ, and 4. The factor n−1/pn^{-1/p}n−1/p in ApA_pAp​ explains why its monotonicity goes in the other direction.

Mean absolute deviation is a different estimand¶

Proposition 8 (Mean absolute deviation and standard deviation)

Let XXX be real with E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞ and μ=EX\mu=\mathbb EXμ=EX. Then E∣X−μ∣≤E∣X∣+∣μ∣<∞\mathbb E|X-\mu|\le\mathbb E|X|+|\mu|<\inftyE∣X−μ∣≤E∣X∣+∣μ∣<∞. If Var⁡(X)<∞\operatorname{Var}(X)<\inftyVar(X)<∞, then E∣X−μ∣≤Var⁡(X)\mathbb E|X-\mu|\le\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}E∣X−μ∣≤Var(X)​, with equality exactly when ∣X−μ∣|X-\mu|∣X−μ∣ is constant almost surely.

Proof 10

The first bound is the triangle inequality in expectation. For the second, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to ∣X−μ∣|X-\mu|∣X−μ∣ and the constant 1. Its equality condition is precisely that ∣X−μ∣|X-\mu|∣X−μ∣ be constant almost surely, including the degenerate case.

These are unscaled deviations; Gaussian calibration multiplies the mean absolute deviation by π/2\sqrt{\pi/2}π/2​, so that universal inequality does not apply to the calibrated value.

For example, the symmetric law on {−1,1}\{-1,1\}{−1,1} has standard deviation and unscaled mean absolute deviation both equal to 1. Its Gaussian-calibrated Std/MeanAD ratio is 2/π<1\sqrt{2/\pi}<12/π​<1. The Gaussian benchmark 1 in the dispersion diagnostic is a model reference, not a universal lower bound. Mean and median absolute deviations also answer different questions. Neither universally replaces a second-moment estimand or dominates every estimator under every loss.

Matching a Gaussian sample by absolute error¶

For iid integrable observations with mean μ\muμ, let M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣ and assume M(1)>0M(1)>0M(1)>0. The kappa note compares this sum deviation at two sizes. Here the target is the relative mean absolute error of the sample mean:

$$

R(n)=\frac{M(n)}{nM(1)}. $$

Scaling two parent laws to the same single-observation MAD makes R(n)R(n)R(n) a comparison in common units. For a Gaussian sample of size ngn_gng​, this relative error is ng−1/2n_g^{-1/2}ng−1/2​. Define the minimum matching integer by

$$

n_*=\min{n\in\mathbb N:n\ge1,\ R(n)\le n_g^{-1/2}}. $$

This criterion matches one expectation of an estimation error. It does not equate variances, quantiles, or confidence coverage. For example, the corresponding probability bound is only Markov’s inequality.

Proposition 9 (A probability bound from expected absolute error)

For iid integrable XiX_iXi​ with mean μ\muμ, let Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​ and M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣. For every n≥1n\ge1n≥1 and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, P(∣Xˉn−μ∣>ε)≤M(n)/(nε)P(|\bar X_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\le M(n)/(n\varepsilon)P(∣Xˉn​−μ∣>ε)≤M(n)/(nε).

Proof 11

Apply Markov’s inequality to ∣Xˉn−μ∣|\bar X_n-\mu|∣Xˉn​−μ∣, whose expectation is M(n)/nM(n)/nM(n)/n.

The bound may be loose. There is no universal kappa cutoff that certifies a normal confidence interval. Under variance matching, every iid law with the same finite variance has the same variance of its sample mean at the same size; that is a different comparison.

Why the search is valid¶

We justify the population search using monotonicity and convergence.

Lemma 1 (Existence of a Gaussian absolute-error match)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid integrable observations with mean μ\muμ and M(1)=E∣X1−μ∣>0M(1)=\mathbb E|X_1-\mu|>0M(1)=E∣X1​−μ∣>0. Define M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣ and R(n)=M(n)/(nM(1))R(n)=M(n)/(nM(1))R(n)=M(n)/(nM(1)). Then E∣Xˉn−μ∣=M(n)/n\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|=M(n)/nE∣Xˉn​−μ∣=M(n)/n is nonincreasing and tends to zero, and so does R(n)R(n)R(n). For every finite integer ng≥1n_g\ge1ng​≥1, the set {n≥1:R(n)≤ng−1/2}\{n\ge1:R(n)\le n_g^{-1/2}\}{n≥1:R(n)≤ng−1/2​} is nonempty and has a finite smallest integer n∗n_*n∗​.

Proof 12

Center n+1n+1n+1 observations and form the n+1n+1n+1 averages that each omit one observation. Their average is the full (n+1)(n+1)(n+1)-observation average. Convexity of absolute value and identical distributions therefore give

E∣Xˉn+1−μ∣≤E∣Xˉn−μ∣.\mathbb E|\bar X_{n+1}-\mu| \le\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|.E∣Xˉn+1​−μ∣≤E∣Xˉn​−μ∣.
(8)

It also tends to zero under integrability. To see this, clip each centered variable to [−B,B][-B,B][−B,B] and center the clipped variable again. Its average has expected absolute value at most its standard deviation divided by n\sqrt nn​. The remaining centered part has expected absolute value at most twice the expected clipping error, uniformly in nnn, and this tends to zero as B→∞B\to\inftyB→∞. First take n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, then B→∞B\to\inftyB→∞. Thus n∗n_*n∗​ exists for every finite integer ngn_gng​ under these assumptions.

A finite computational search can still stop before reaching it.

Use gaussian_equivalent_n with deterministic population MADs, such as student_sum_mad and gamma_sum_mad.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import gaussian_equivalent_n, student_sum_mad, gamma_sum_mad

target = 1/30**0.5
print(f"Gaussian target: {target:.4f}")
for name, mad in (("Student 3", student_sum_mad), ("Exponential", gamma_sum_mad)):
    n = gaussian_equivalent_n(mad, 30)
    print(f"{name}: n={n}")
    for j in (n-1, n):
        print(f"  n={j}: relative error={mad(j)/(j*mad(1)):.4f}")
print("Cap at 10:", gaussian_equivalent_n(student_sum_mad, 30, max_n=10))

Output

Gaussian target: 0.1826
Student 3: n=44
  n=43: relative error=0.1837
  n=44: relative error=0.1817
Exponential: n=36
  n=35: relative error=0.1829
  n=36: relative error=0.1803
Cap at 10: None

The cap result means only that the requested finite search did not find a match. A noisy Monte Carlo curve must not be passed to this binary search: sampling noise can destroy monotonicity and shift the first crossing.

When a constant kappa is enough¶

Corollary 3 (Exact sample-size matching under a constant kappa)

Under the assumptions of Lemma 1, suppose M(n)/M(1)=n1/(2−κ)M(n)/M(1)=n^{1/(2-\kappa)}M(n)/M(1)=n1/(2−κ) at every integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1, for a fixed κ<1\kappa<1κ<1. Then for every integer ng≥1n_g\ge1ng​≥1,

$$

n_*=\left\lceil n_g^{,(2-\kappa)/[2(1-\kappa)]}\right\rceil. $$

For an integrable nondegenerate stable law of index 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2, κ=2−α\kappa=2-\alphaκ=2−α, giving exponent α/[2(α−1)]\alpha/[2(\alpha-1)]α/[2(α−1)].

Proof 13

Substitution gives R(n)=n−(1−κ)/(2−κ)R(n)=n^{-(1-\kappa)/(2-\kappa)}R(n)=n−(1−κ)/(2−κ). Its exponent is negative, so R(n)≤ng−1/2R(n)\le n_g^{-1/2}R(n)≤ng−1/2​ is equivalent to n≥ng(2−κ)/[2(1−κ)]n\ge n_g^{(2-\kappa)/[2(1-\kappa)]}n≥ng(2−κ)/[2(1−κ)]​. Taking the smallest integer gives the ceiling. The stable kappa formula Corollary 1 gives the last assertion.

At α=1.5\alpha=1.5α=1.5, this exponent is 1.5.

For a general law, substituting a small-size kappa into this formula is a heuristic. Its kappa changes with size, so the exact equation is implicit. The cubic Student and exponential examples use their full MAD curves.

Equal-weight exposures and apparent stabilization¶

For independent, identically distributed centered exposures Xi−μX_i-\muXi​−μ, the equally weighted portfolio fluctuation is n−1∑i(Xi−μ)n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\mu)n−1∑i​(Xi​−μ). Its MAD is exactly M(n)/nM(n)/nM(n)/n. The aggregation figure therefore also quantifies this narrowly specified diversification calculation. A smooth sample path or a visually concentrated center can still conceal substantial expected absolute error.

Corollary 4 (A common component survives averaging)

Let CCC be integrable, independent of iid centered integrable ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​, and set Xi=C+ϵiX_i=C+\epsilon_iXi​=C+ϵi​. Then Xˉn→C\bar X_n\to CXˉn​→C in L1L^1L1 and E∣Xˉn−EC∣→E∣C−EC∣\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mathbb EC|\to\mathbb E|C-\mathbb EC|E∣Xˉn​−EC∣→E∣C−EC∣. If ϵi=0\epsilon_i=0ϵi​=0 almost surely, the average is exactly CCC at every size.

Proof 14

The clipping argument in Lemma 1 gives E∣n−1∑iϵi∣→0\mathbb E|n^{-1}\sum_i\epsilon_i|\to0E∣n−1∑i​ϵi​∣→0. If the deviations are identically zero this is immediate; otherwise the lemma applies with positive normalization. Since Xˉn−C=n−1∑iϵi\bar X_n-C=n^{-1}\sum_i\epsilon_iXˉn​−C=n−1∑i​ϵi​, this is L1L^1L1 convergence. The reverse triangle inequality bounds the difference of the two MADs by E∣Xˉn−C∣\mathbb E|\bar X_n-C|E∣Xˉn​−C∣.

Increasing the number of components cannot remove the common fluctuation.

These model identities are the scope used for Taleb (2025), §§8.3.2/8.5, pp. 159–164. They do not establish an optimal allocation, a universal risk multiple, or empirical kappa values for stocks. For different weights and dependence, return to the multivariate note and shared-shock example.

Reproduce the moment-estimation experiment¶

Use pareto_type1, pareto_moment_estimator_summary.

Code
import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.distributions import pareto_type1
from xmath.incerto.finite_moments import pareto_moment_estimator_summary

rng = np.random.default_rng(20261020)
for alpha in (3, 6):
    sample = pareto_type1.rvs(alpha, size=(100, 200), random_state=rng)
    estimates = np.mean(sample**2, axis=1)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:.4g}")
    for name, value in pareto_moment_estimator_summary(alpha, q=2, n=200).items():
        print(f"  {name}: {value:.4g}")
    quantiles = np.quantile(estimates, [0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
    print("Sample quantiles: [" + ", ".join(f"{v:.4g}" for v in quantiles) + "]")

Output

alpha=3
  moment: 3
  estimator_variance: inf
Sample quantiles: [2.335, 2.726, 3.491]
alpha=6
  moment: 1.5
  estimator_variance: 0.00375
Sample quantiles: [1.433, 1.497, 1.592]

The quantiles describe 100 seeded second-moment estimates from samples of size 200.

Figure regeneration: uv run python demos/incerto/finite_moments.py. NumPy’s PCG64 generator uses seed 20261018; sample sizes are 50, 200, 1000, and 5000, with 600 independent replications per law and size. The four laws are unit normal, the stated rare-state mixture, and Pareto with xm=1x_m=1xm​=1, α=3,6\alpha=3,6α=3,6. The script allocates one sample size at a time, about 3 million observations at the largest size, and normally takes seconds. It performs no clipping, censoring, external-data access, or silent non-finite removal.

The experiment illustrates finite-sample spread. The proofs above establish moment boundaries; a finite Monte Carlo variance cannot test an infinite population variance. Later chapters develop convergence rates and broader comparisons. The Cauchy running-statistics experiment belongs to chapter 7.
